title: Marketing Attribution: A Practical Guide to Choosing and Validating a Model
description: A practical framework for defining conversions, choosing attribution models, validating tracking, and applying evaluation criteria without overstating what the data proves.
author: PilotStack Team

sections.title: Start With the Decision, Not the Dashboard
sections.body: Attribution assigns credit for a conversion across the marketing interactions recorded before it. It is not a complete record of why a person bought. Before choosing a platform or model, write down the decision the report must support: reallocating paid spend, understanding assisted conversions, evaluating content, or comparing lead-generation channels. Define the conversion event, reporting period, currency, and decision owner. If sales-qualified leads and purchases are both important, report them separately instead of combining them into one ambiguous conversion total.

sections.title: Choose a Model That Matches the Question
sections.body: Last-click is simple and useful for understanding the final recorded touchpoint, but it can under-credit awareness and research. First-click highlights discovery but can over-credit the first interaction. Linear models spread credit across recorded touches; position-based models give extra weight to selected stages; time-decay models favor interactions nearer to conversion. Data-driven models estimate contribution from observed paths, but depend on data volume, tracking quality, and the vendor's methodology. Pick a primary model for a defined decision and keep a second view for context. Do not present model-assigned credit as proof of incremental impact.

sections.title: Audit Measurement Before Comparing Channels
sections.body: Create a measurement map with one row per conversion: event name, trigger, destination, deduplication rule, consent requirement, owner, and validation method. Check that a purchase fires once to prevent double-counted conversions, values and currencies are consistent, form submissions are not counted again on a thank-you-page refresh, and cross-domain and cross-device journeys are handled intentionally. Document gaps caused by consent choices, browser restrictions, offline sales, ad blockers, or untagged links. If tracking changed mid-period, mark it in the report; a change in recorded conversions may reflect instrumentation rather than demand.

sections.title: Standardize Campaign Naming and UTMs
sections.body: Define a naming convention for source, medium, campaign, content, and term, then publish examples the whole team can follow. Use lowercase values and a controlled list of channel names; avoid creating new spellings for the same source in every campaign. Never put personal or sensitive information in a URL parameter. Test tagged links from the first click through the final event and check whether redirects strip parameters. Keep a change log so historical reports remain interpretable when naming rules evolve.

sections.title: Build a Channel Report That Shows Its Limits
sections.body: For each channel, show spend where available, recorded conversions, conversion value, cost per conversion, and the attribution model used. Separate first-touch, last-touch, and assisted views when each answers a different question. Include data-quality notes for missing spend, incomplete offline conversion imports, consent-related gaps, and channels that cannot be compared fairly. Do not compare revenue attributed by one system with spend recorded under a different date window or currency without reconciling definitions. Annotate launches, promotions, tracking outages, and major budget changes.

sections.title: Estimate Incrementality With a Separate Test
sections.body: Attribution describes observed journeys; incrementality asks what would have happened without the marketing activity. When budget and audience allow, use a holdout, geographic test, or carefully designed experiment with a pre-defined primary metric and test window. Avoid changing several channels and the landing page at once if you need to identify what caused a result. Record the design, eligibility rules, sample limitations, and uncertainty. If a controlled test is not feasible, label the conclusion as directional rather than claiming attributed conversions were all caused by the campaign.

sections.title: A 30-Day Implementation Checklist
sections.body: Week one: agree on conversion definitions, reporting ownership, and the tracking map. Week two: audit events, UTMs, consent behavior, deduplication, and cross-domain journeys; fix the highest-impact gaps first. Week three: publish one dashboard with the model and definitions visible, then reconcile a sample of conversions against source records. Week four: review the report with marketing and sales, list unresolved gaps, and choose one experiment or instrumentation improvement. Document what the report can support, what it cannot support, and when the model or definitions should be reviewed again.
